locator.quote: Ultimately, for Poet, lighting design remains less about how many possibilities a fixture can offer than knowing which possibilities to use. locator.quote: “It’s such a crazy thing. I think it’s a wild job because sound design barely even exists. It only happens when the show is happening, right? And for most of the show, we’re not making sound. We’re just taking the sound that everybody else makes, all the performers, and then we basically just set the relative volumes of it and send it out to the speakers to the audience at relative volume levels depending where they’re sitting and what they need.”

locator.quote: “It’s almost like curating exactly what the audience should be hearing out of everything that’s done on stage,” explained Trarbach. “We put microphones on every actor, every musician. I think there may be like 18 or 20 microphones in the percussion area alone because they’ve got all these little things. Then we just kind of take it moment by moment and we try to mix the songs, try and make them sound a little better every time we do it.”

locator.quote: “I think the microphone has actually helped actors give a lot more sensitive performances, which is a great thing about it,” said Trarbach. “But we made the design decision early on that we didn’t want it to sound produced or slick or like a modern musical sound. We wanted it to be very open and expansive and focus on just what the performers were doing and presenting that to the audience.”

locator.quote: AC: All the theaters are so unique. And it depends on what type of theater it is. When I say that, I mean, is it a grid theater that has a fixed grid above, or is it a fly house that has a fly rail where you could bring scenery in and out from above? Is it in the round? Is it alley? Most designers would say they design for the space. You’re designing for the play, of course, but you also design for the space. What I mean by that is the size of the theater. An Importance of Being Earnest on an 80 foot wide theater is going to look very different from an Importance of Being Earnest that’s in a 20 foot wide thrust theater. You also want to fit the space, the set wants to fit nicely in the space as well. And with all that being said, the goal for us is always to focus on the actors. So a lot of the time in these bigger theaters, our goal is to focus in, to really keep our eye where the action is, which is the actors in the play.

claim: Set designers begin by reading scripts multiple times from different perspectives, annotating stage directions and character cues, followed by discussions with directors to align on story flow and visual interpretation, involving extensive research and collaboration to adapt designs for unique theatre spaces.
source_title: Andrew Cohen: A Behind the Scenes on Set Design

locator.quote: AC: My typical process is usually the same across the board. I’ll get the script and I’ll read it. Usually for fun, but I also write down some stuff that I will want to remember, any important stage directions, or anything a character says about where they are or what they’re about to do or where they’re going that may not be in the stage directions. Sometimes that is left out of the stage directions and something happens with what a character says. So I’ll read the script and I’ll jot down some notes and then I’ll talk with the director. We’ll have a conversation about how we want to approach it, what do we think it looks like, and how does it work? I might get into a little more specifics at the time, like “ I was thinking the front door is on the right side of the stage? Do you agree with that?” You know, some of these basic questions like,”How do we want this play to flow?” Then maybe, depending on the play and how– I don’t want to say straightforward– but straightforward, the play or the musical is, I may have some research I’ve already pulled that I found, of what I think the set or location may look like. A lot of inspiration, period research and stuff like that, just to have some things to show the director and for us to say “Oh, it looks more like this thing and not like that thing,” which is really helpful because then I could gather more of this idea to really supplement what I’m going to do with it.

locator.quote: Training excludes the validation and test assets and contains approximately 150 minutes of paired music and lighting cues. Validation covers six styles with two held-out examples per scenario and supplies manual references for the main-paper comparison. Test uses six unseen tracks across the six styles on a stage excluded from training. This is a controlled, style-balanced check of unseen music and unseen stage layout, not a population-scale benchmark; full-length expert/non-expert scoring limits its practical sample size. A cue-statistic t-SNE analysis over 14 stage-level output vectors yields a mean pairwise z-scored distance of 5.409±1.7465.409\pm 1.746, indicating multiple statistic regimes rather than collapse to a single template. The real-world demo stage is unseen; its nearest cue-statistic neighbors are the dance and rock stage cases. Because the t-SNE uses available cue-output vectors rather than the complete raw Musilux corpus, we treat it as supplementary descriptive evidence, not as a standalone generalization metric.

claim: AI systems like AuraLuxMuse use deep learning to generate stylistically diverse, music-driven lighting cues by aligning audio and lighting parameters and providing preference conditioning through expert ensembles, indicating potential for design assistance but facing challenges in parameterization, personalization, and evaluation.
source_title: AuraLuxMuse: Adaptive Fusion Modeling for Aesthetic Stage Lighting Design with Music and Expert Guidance

locator.quote: At the heart of AuraLuxMuse are two key modules: Lighting-Aligned Music Pretraining (LAMP), which performs contrastive learning between audio and lighting cues for alignment, and Preference-Adaptive Mixture of Experts (PAMoE), which conditions preference-aware cue retrieval and adaptation on designers’ intent through a gated ensemble of style-specific expert networks. To support training and evaluation, we introduce Musilux, the first dataset of paired musical audio and professional lighting cue sequences under diverse performance scenarios. We evaluate AuraLuxMuse across both virtual simulation environments and professional-grade laboratories. Experimental results, including objective and subjective evaluation, demonstrate that AuraLuxMuse retrieves and adapts stage-lighting cues that are visually cohesive, semantically meaningful, and artistically expressive, showing its potential for AI-assisted aesthetic stage design.

claim: AI systems like AuraLuxMuse use deep learning to generate stylistically diverse, music-driven lighting cues by aligning audio and lighting parameters and providing preference conditioning through expert ensembles, indicating potential for design assistance but facing challenges in parameterization, personalization, and evaluation.
source_title: AuraLuxMuse: Adaptive Fusion Modeling for Aesthetic Stage Lighting Design with Music and Expert Guidance

locator.quote: Consequently, there is a compelling need for a system capable of modeling and automating the entire stage lighting design process. However, existing machine-learning systems typically restrict lighting control to basic properties such as light position and intensity, overlooking critical expressive dimensions including color, stylistic variation, and temporal rhythm. To the best of our knowledge, this topic has not been systematically explored under modern deep-learning paradigms. With advances in deep audio representation learning, it is now feasible to encode the latent structure of music in high-dimensional embedding spaces, providing a promising foundation for music-driven lighting synthesis. Three key challenges remain. The first is lack of structured parameterization: there is no standardized formulation for decomposing lighting attributes into learnable parameters. The second is multimodal alignment and personalization: learning effective correspondences between music and lighting remains difficult, particularly when integrating personalized and stylistic preferences. The third is the absence of comprehensive evaluation metrics: existing benchmarks fail to assess lighting quality in terms of both objective fidelity and subjective perception.

claim: AI systems like AuraLuxMuse use deep learning to generate stylistically diverse, music-driven lighting cues by aligning audio and lighting parameters and providing preference conditioning through expert ensembles, indicating potential for design assistance but facing challenges in parameterization, personalization, and evaluation.
source_title: AuraLuxMuse: Adaptive Fusion Modeling for Aesthetic Stage Lighting Design with Music and Expert Guidance

locator.quote: Because lighting-cue generation has not previously been formulated as a sequence-to-sequence task, we introduce a custom CueTokenizer to bridge continuous VGGish audio features and structured lighting controls. It converts lighting events into token sequences by quantizing continuous parameters into 256 bins and mapping categorical attributes to an NLP-like vocabulary. Using this formulation, we train four autoregressive baselines with token-level cross-entropy and teacher forcing: lightweight adaptations of BART (Lewis et al., 2019) and T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), which inject linearly projected audio frames as encoder embeddings; a domain-specific SpecTNT (Lu et al., 2021) surrogate with a lightweight causal Transformer decoder; and an Autoformer (Wu et al., 2022) surrogate with a higher-capacity sequence-modeling variant.
